s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 August 2026
m: Published real-time figure
did: Took over 84 Lumber from her father Joe Hardy in 1992 at age 26 and rebuilt it around contractor supply rather than consumer walk-in, growing it to 320 stores in 34 states and over 5 billion dollars of revenue; also owns the Nemacolin resort in Farmington, Pennsylvania.
why: 84 Lumber sells to professional builders on credit and stocks components rather than retail SKUs, so it rides housing starts without competing on price with Home Depot. Staying private meant she could keep opening stores through downturns when public rivals had to protect quarterly margins.
obst: The 2007-2011 housing collapse cut 84 Lumber revenue by roughly two thirds and forced her to close about 250 of 450 stores; she took no outside capital and rebuilt store count over the following decade.
turn: The 2009 decision to shut half the store base and refocus entirely on professional builders rather than defend consumer retail square footage.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 August 2026
m: Published real-time figure
did: A CERN-trained particle physicist who founded Vicor in Andover, Massachusetts in 1981 to build zero-current-switching DC-DC power converters, and still runs it as chairman and CEO with more than 150 patents; he holds roughly 8.8 million shares, about a fifth of the company.
why: Vicor patented the high-frequency switching topologies that let a converter shrink by an order of magnitude, then refused to license them cheaply. When AI racks moved to 48-volt power distribution, the vertical power modules Vicor had spent forty years patenting became the only qualified part.
obst: Vicor spent the 2000s in patent litigation against SynQor and others over power-converter claims, and its stock lost more than two thirds of its value in 2022-2023 as datacenter customers delayed the 48-volt transition before AI demand reversed it.
turn: The 2023-2026 AI datacenter buildout, when hyperscaler rack power moved to the 48-volt architecture Vicor had been selling into a market that did not yet exist.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 August 2026
m: Published real-time figure
did: Founded InterSystems in 1978 and still owns 100 percent of it; its Cache and IRIS object databases sit under Epic, Veterans Affairs VistA and much of the electronic health record installed base, generating roughly a billion dollars a year with no outside shareholders.
why: InterSystems sells the database engine to the companies that sell the hospital software, so it collects a royalty on health IT without ever having to win a hospital sales cycle. Never raising capital meant no pressure to sell into the 1990s relational database consolidation that killed its peers.
obst: The industry moved to SQL relational databases in the 1990s and treated the MUMPS-derived object model as a legacy dead end; InterSystems had to keep its own ecosystem alive for two decades against near-universal analyst hostility.
turn: Epic Systems standardising its entire product on Cache, which turned InterSystems into the substrate for a large share of US patient records as Epic won hospital after hospital.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 August 2026

why: Everyone else was a generalist buyout shop. Owning only media and communications meant Providence could underwrite subscriber churn and spectrum value faster than a generalist committee, and sellers in those sectors called them first.
obst: The firm was badly exposed to print and broadcast as advertising moved online, and its 2007-vintage fund carried leveraged media assets straight into the 2008 credit freeze.
turn: The 2007 ZeniMax investment, which returned roughly six times when Microsoft bought the Bethesda parent in 2021 and validated the decision to keep buying content rather than distribution.

obst: Dexter Shoe collapsed under low-cost Asian manufacturing and was folded into H.H. Brown by 2001, wiping out the business itself; her youngest brother Peter died of malaria in 2017.
turn: The 1993 decision to take Berkshire Hathaway stock rather than cash for Dexter, which converted a doomed shoe company into a compounding equity stake.

turn: His 2012 return as CEO after Glen Senk left, when he cut the Urban brand back and pushed capital into Anthropologie, Free People and the Nuuly rental service instead.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 August 2026

why: Flagship owns the company at inception instead of buying into a priced round, so the entry basis is near zero and there is no founder to negotiate with. Killing hypotheses inside the lab before incorporation meant Flagship paid for failure at a hundred thousand dollars rather than a Series A.
obst: Moderna could not raise a conventional biotech round for years because no messenger RNA drug had ever been approved and the technology had been abandoned by others over immunogenicity; Flagship funded it internally through that gap.
turn: The January 2020 decision to build a vaccine against a sequence posted online, which put Moderna into human trials 63 days later and made mRNA a platform rather than a thesis.

did: MIT chemical engineer who co-founded Moderna in 2010 with Flagship after his lab established controlled-release polymer delivery; he holds roughly 3 percent of the company and has co-founded more than 40 others including Alkermes, Living Proof and Frequency Therapeutics.
why: The Moderna problem was never the messenger RNA sequence, it was getting it into a cell without triggering immunity or degrading. obst: His first nine grant applications were rejected and his early polymer work was publicly attacked as impossible by established chemists; Moderna shares fell from 4.9 billion dollars of his paper wealth in 2021 to 343 million by January 2026 before recovering.
turn: The August 2026 late-stage melanoma vaccine readout with Merck's Keytruda, which sent Moderna up 156 percent to about 161 dollars and restored his stake to ten figures.

turn: The 2018 FDA approval of Onpattro for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis, the first approved RNAi drug, sixteen years after founding and after the entire sector had been written off.
